AbstractText.Label: UNLABELLED
AbstractText.content: The stress of being a doctor and being responsible for own decisions is one of the most intense feelings the doctors have to cope with. The stress coping styles are determined by the factors dependent on psychological variables such as personality.

AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: The aim of study was to assess the relation between personality traits and stress coping among physicians.

AbstractText.Label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
AbstractText.content: The study group consisted of 50 physicians (males n=25; 50%) employed in Norbert Barlicki Memorial Medical University Teaching Hospital No 1 in Lodz. The stress coping styles were assessed using Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations, whereas the tool used for personality assessment was NEO Five Factor Inventory of Personality.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Task-oriented coping (TOC) was the predominant stress coping style among physicians (mean sten value 6.7±2.0; high sten scores - 8-10 in 38%). Among all dimensions of the doctors' personality, extraversion predominated significantly (mean sten value 9.7±0.7). Neuroticism correlated positively with emotional oriented coping (EOC) (r=0.43). Extraversion influenced more infrequent adoption of EOC by males (r=-0.43) and older subjects (≥44years) (r=-0.52). Conscientiousness influenced more frequent adoption of TOC by females (r=0.46). Both the doctors' age (r=-0.49 p<0.05)), and duration of employment (r=-0.49 p<0.05)) significantly correlated negatively with AOC. The doctors' gender did not affect their stress coping styles.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Task oriented coping was the dominant stress coping style among physicians. High levels of neuroticism correlated positively, and those of extraversion negatively with the adoption of emotional oriented coping with stress. The tendency to choose the avoidance oriented coping decreases with the physicians' age and duration of employment.
